newsitem.title: UK: Amnesty condemns human rights abuses in Algeria.
newsitem.headline: Amnesty condemns human rights abuses in Algeria.

text.p: Human rights group Amnesty International condemned both security forces and Moslem rebels in Algeria on Tuesday, accusing them of continued human rights abuses on a wide scale.

"The rule of law no longer exists in Algeria, where an atmosphere of terror and lawlessness holds sway," secretary-general Pierre Sane said in a statement released with a 43-page report entitled "Algeria -- Silence and Fear".
At least 50,000 people have died since authorities annulled 1992 elections in the North African nation which fundamentalists looked set to win, the report said.
"Extrajudicial killings, deliberate and arbitrary murders, "disappearances', torture, kidnappings and death threats are part of daily life in Algeria; and this list is not exhaustive," it said.
"Security forces and armed opposition groups display a profound scorn of the the most fundamental right of the civil population: the right to life," it said.

Sane said human rights abuses were an integral part of the strategy of both security forces and opposition groups despite repeated claims by Algiers that human rights are respected and that the security situation has improved.

The report urged security forces, government-backed militias and rebels to stop the killings. It said that, as far as it was aware, no member of the security forces had ever been investigated for a violation of human rights.
It said the Algiers government should, among other measures:
-- state publicly that crimes ranging from extrajudicial killings to torture would not be tolerated and that security forces would be prosecuted for any abuses
-- set up an independent commission to investigate abuses since 1992, and allow it to publish its conclusions
-- end secret detention of suspects by bolstering the judicial rights of detainees and free anyone now held illegally
-- outlaw confessions obtained under torture from court testimony
-- revise the criminal code to comply with international treaties on human rights signed by Algiers
Amnesty reiterated calls to the rebels for an immediate end to deliberate killings and kidnappings of civilians, a halt to abductions, rapes and other attacks on women and death threats on civilians.
"Such atrocities have created an atmosphere of terror, where people fear not just being killed, but being killed in particularly brutal ways," Sane said.
Western diplomats say the best evidence available suggests that between 150 and 200 people were being killed in Algeria each week.
